# Sharp Fréchet–Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
## 1 Introduction
Even when population marginal distributions are known from auxiliary information, they do not determine the dependence among outcomes. The classical Fréchet–Hoeffding (FH) inequalities (Hoeffding 1940; Fréchet 1951) provide sharp bounds using these marginals alone. But incomplete records contain additional information: they reveal which outcomes are observed and their realized values. Can this information sharpen the classical bounds without imposing restrictions on the observation mechanism?
I consider the identifying content of a different combination of information: known population marginals and the complete observed-data law under unrestricted outcome-dependent observation patterns. The objective is to characterize the resulting sharp FH bounds explicitly and determine when incomplete records improve upon the classical inequalities.
I study a multivariate outcome X=(X_1,…,X_d) whose coordinates are observed according to a random subset S⊆{1,…,d}. For every observation pattern T, the observed-data law identifies the subdistribution μ_T(B)=ℙ(S=T,X_T∈B), while the population marginals F_j are known. I impose no restrictions on the dependence between S and X. The first result establishes an exact reduction of the identification problem to a finite allocation problem for binary threshold indicators.
Every feasible binary allocation can be lifted to a compatible full-data distribution preserving both the original marginal laws and the entire observed subdistributions; equivalently, the mapping from admissible full-data laws to feasible binary allocations is surjective. Consequently, the reduction yields sharp bounds for arbitrary binary-profile scores, even when the underlying outcomes are continuous.

## 原文摘要

Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

# Sharp Fr\'echet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation

## Author

Listed:

- Rami V. Tabri

## Abstract

Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fr\'echet--Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

keenable.title: Sharp Fréchet--Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation
keenable.snippet:
A central difficulty is sample selectivity: whether an outcome is observed may depend on its value or on other, unobserved outcomes. Consequently, the distribution of observed records need not be representative of the population, complicating identification of the joint outcome distribution (Heckman 1979; Manski 1989). Even when population marginal distributions are known from auxiliary information, they do not determine the dependence among outcomes. The classical Fréchet–Hoeffding (FH) inequalities (Hoeffding 1940; Fréchet 1951) provide sharp bounds using these marginals alone. But incomplete records contain additional information: they reveal which outcomes are observed and their realized values. Can this information sharpen the classical bounds without imposing restrictions on the observation mechanism?

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.1, at every fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the sharp lower bound is
$$\underline{H}(x)=\max_{J\subseteq[d]}\left\{\sum_{T:M(T)\subseteq J}a_{T}-\sum_{j\in J}r_{j}^{0}\right\}.$$
The sharp upper bound is the optimal value of the fractional packing problem
$$\overline{H}(x)=\max\left\{\sum_{T\subseteq[d]}t_{T}:\begin{array}[]{l}0\leq t_{T}\leq a_{T}\quad(T\subseteq[d]),\\[2.0pt]
\displaystyle\sum_{T:j\in M(T)}t_{T}\leq r_{j}^{1}\quad(j\in[d])\end{array}\right\}.$$
Equivalently, the upper bound has the dual representation
$$\overline{H}(x)=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_{j}r_{j}^{1}+\sum_{T\subseteq[d]}a_{T}\left(1-\sum_{j\in M(T)}\lambda_{j}\right)_{+}\right\},$$
where $(u)_{+}=\max\{u,0\}$. All extrema are attained, and the bounds are sharp for the original real-valued observation model without restrictions on the dependence between $X$ and $S$.

For comparison, the classical pointwise Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds using the marginal probabilities alone are
$$L_{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=\max\left\{0,\sum_{j=1}^{d}q_{j}-(d-1)\right\},\qquad U_{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=\min_{j\in[d]}q_{j}.$$

keenable.title: Sharp upper and lower bounds on the variance of U-statistics
keenable.snippet: For a U-statistic with a symmetric kernel of any rank, we offer new upper and lower bounds on its variance, which are uniformly sharper than those established in the classical paper by Hoeffding (1948, Theorem 5.2). Our new bounds have strong optimality properties and can tightly describe how the variance scales with the degree of the kernel. As an application, we leverage our new upper bound to improve an existing Berry-Esseen theorem for the normal approximation of incomplete U-statistics based on Bernoulli sampling, in a computationally frugal regime where the computational budget is much smaller than the available sample size.

keenable.title: Bounding MrP: Subnational public opinion estimation without detailed census data
keenable.snippet:
Multilevel regression with post-stratification (MrP) is the dominant method for estimating public opinion in subnational units. The method requires the full joint distribution of demographic variables in a subnational unit, which is often unavailable from public census tabulations. Existing approaches fill this gap by imposing assumptions to combine marginal distributions of census variables into a synthetic joint distribution. We propose sharp MrP bounds instead: the smallest interval containing all estimates of subnational public opinion consistent with the marginal distributions alone. The bounds solve a pair of linear programs and are computationally feasible for typical applications in political science. Applied to two prominent examples in the literature, the bounds are tight enough to be informative and often more accurate than MrP restricted to a coarser, observed joint distribution of census variables. The bounds serve as margin-consistent interval estimates and a diagnostic when researchers use a synthetic joint distribution to construct MrP estimates.

As we show in Appendix A.2, the interval is sharp, i.e., every value inside is attained by some π consistent with the observed margins, and no value outside is attained. It is also the smallest possible interval that does not rely on assumptions beyond those imposed by the observed marginal distributions. The same logic underlies the classical Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds on a joint distribution with fixed marginals (Fréchet, 1951; Hoeffding, 1940; Rüschendorf, 1991).

keenable.title: Treatment Evaluation at the Intensive and Extensive Margins
keenable.snippet:
This paper provides a solution to the evaluation of treatment effects in selec-
tive samples when neither instruments nor parametric assumptions are available.
We provide sharp bounds for average treatment effects under a conditional mono-
tonicity assumption for all principal strata, i.e. units characterizing the complete
intensive and extensive margins. Most importantly, we allow for a large share of
units whose selection is indifferent to treatment, e.g. due to non-compliance. The
existence of such a population is crucially tied to the regularity of sharp popula-
tion bounds and thus conventional asymptotic inference for methods such as Lee
bounds can be misleading. This problem can be solved using smoothed outer iden-
tification regions for inference. We provide semiparametrically efficient debiased
machine learning estimators for both regular and smooth bounds that can accom-
modate high-dimensional covariates and flexible functional forms.

1 Introduction
Many questions in empirical economics concern the joint behavior of outcomes that are not fully observed. Examples include income persistence across generations, dependence between potential outcomes, and multidimensional economic deprivation. Sample selectivity arises when whether an outcome is observed depends on its value or on other, unobserved outcomes. Consequently, the distribution of observed records need not be representative of the population, complicating identification of the joint outcome distribution (Heckman 1979; Manski 1989). Even when population marginal distributions are known from auxiliary information, they do not determine the dependence among outcomes. The classical Fréchet–Hoeffding (FH) inequalities (Hoeffding 1940; Fréchet 1951) provide sharp bounds using these marginals alone. But incomplete records contain additional information: they reveal which outcomes are observed and their realized values.

## Sharp Fréchet–Hoeffding Bounds under Selectively Incomplete Observation

Rami V. Tabri Note: Department of Econometrics and Business Statistics, Monash University. Email: rami.tabri@monash.edu.

###### Abstract

Incomplete records can sharpen bounds on joint outcome probabilities even when no pair of outcomes is jointly observed. I derive sharp pointwise Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds combining known population marginals with selectively observed records, without restricting the observation mechanism. I establish an exact reduction of the identification problem to finite-dimensional optimization, yielding computable characterizations of both bounds. Illustrations involving income mobility, potential outcomes, and split questionnaires demonstrate how incomplete records can improve identification relative to the classical bounds.

Keywords: Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds; incomplete observations; partial identification; optimal transport; sample selectivity.  
JEL classification: C02, C14, C18.

## 1 Introduction

Many questions in empirical economics concern the joint behavior of outcomes that are not fully observed. Examples include income persistence across generations, dependence between potential outcomes, and multidimensional economic deprivation. Sample selectivity arises when whether an outcome is observed depends on its value or on other, unobserved outcomes. Consequently, the distribution of observed records need not be representative of the population, complicating identification of the joint outcome distribution (Heckman 1979; Manski 1989). Even when population marginal distributions are known from auxiliary information, they do not determine the dependence among outcomes. ## The problem: how far can training error be trusted?

Every classifier in this course was judged, in the end, by a number computed on data we had: a training error, a validation error, a cross-validation average. What we actually care about is different. We want to know how often the classifier will be wrong on points nobody has shown us yet. This lesson asks the question the way a theoretical computer scientist would. Not "how good is this classifier?", but "how many examples must I see before the error I measure is close to the error I will suffer, and how sure can I be of that?" The answer is a **sample complexity**: a number of training examples, as a function of how close and how sure we want to be.

Two quantities need names. Assume the pairs \((x, y)\), an input and its label, are drawn from a fixed distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) that we do not know. The **generalisation error** of a hypothesis \(h\) (a classifier, a decision rule) is the probability that it errs on a fresh pair:

\[ \varepsilon(h) = P_{(x, y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big(h(x) \neq y\big). \]

It is also the expected fraction of mistakes on new data. We never see it. What we see is the **empirical error**, or **empirical risk**, on a training set of \(m\) pairs:

\[ \hat{\varepsilon}(h) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf{1}\{h(x_i) \neq y_i\}, \]

where the indicator \(\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}\) is 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise. So \(\hat{\varepsilon}(h)\) is simply the fraction of training points that \(h\) gets wrong. The whole lesson is about the gap \(|\varepsilon(h) - \hat{\varepsilon}(h)|\). The flavour resembles hypothesis testing from the evaluation lessons, but the analysis here goes a different way: it bounds the gap for many hypotheses at once.

# Testing Monotonicity in a Finite Population

Jiafeng Chen, Jonathan Roth, and Jann Spiess

Abstract. We consider the extent to which we can learn from a completely randomized experiment whether all individuals have treatment effects that are weakly of the same sign, a condition we call monotonicity. In probability theory, **Hoeffding's inequality** provides an upper bound on the probability that the sum of bounded independent random variables deviates from its expected value by more than a certain amount. Hoeffding's inequality was proven by Wassily Hoeffding in 1963.

Hoeffding's inequality is a special case of the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality and McDiarmid's inequality. It is similar to the Chernoff bound, but tends to be less sharp, in particular when the variance of the random variables is small. ultimate.snippet:
A central difficulty is sample selectivity: whether an outcome is observed may depend on its value or on other, unobserved outcomes. Consequently, the distribution of observed records need not be representative of the population, complicating identification of the joint outcome distribution (Heckman 1979; Manski 1989). Even when population marginal distributions are known from auxiliary information, they do not determine the dependence among outcomes. The classical Fréchet–Hoeffding (FH) inequalities (Hoeffding 1940; Fréchet 1951) provide sharp bounds using these marginals alone. But incomplete records contain additional information: they reveal which outcomes are observed and their realized values. Can this information sharpen the classical bounds without imposing restrictions on the observation mechanism?

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.1, at every fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the sharp lower bound is
$$\underline{H}(x)=\max_{J\subseteq[d]}\left\{\sum_{T:M(T)\subseteq J}a_{T}-\sum_{j\in J}r_{j}^{0}\right\}.$$
The sharp upper bound is the optimal value of the fractional packing problem
$$\overline{H}(x)=\max\left\{\sum_{T\subseteq[d]}t_{T}:\begin{array}[]{l}0\leq t_{T}\leq a_{T}\quad(T\subseteq[d]),\\[2.0pt]
\displaystyle\sum_{T:j\in M(T)}t_{T}\leq r_{j}^{1}\quad(j\in[d])\end{array}\right\}.$$
Equivalently, the upper bound has the dual representation
$$\overline{H}(x)=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{d}}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_{j}r_{j}^{1}+\sum_{T\subseteq[d]}a_{T}\left(1-\sum_{j\in M(T)}\lambda_{j}\right)_{+}\right\},$$
where $(u)_{+}=\max\{u,0\}$. All extrema are attained, and the bounds are sharp for the original real-valued observation model without restrictions on the dependence between $X$ and $S$.

For comparison, the classical pointwise Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds using the marginal probabilities alone are
$$L_{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=\max\left\{0,\sum_{j=1}^{d}q_{j}-(d-1)\right\},\qquad U_{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=\min_{j\in[d]}q_{j}.$$

ultimate.snippet: For a U-statistic with a symmetric kernel of any rank, we offer new upper and lower bounds on its variance, which are uniformly sharper than those established in the classical paper by Hoeffding (1948, Theorem 5.2). ultimate.title: Bounding MrP: Subnational public opinion estimation without detailed census data
ultimate.snippet:
Multilevel regression with post-stratification (MrP) is the dominant method for estimating public opinion in subnational units. The method requires the full joint distribution of demographic variables in a subnational unit, which is often unavailable from public census tabulations. Existing approaches fill this gap by imposing assumptions to combine marginal distributions of census variables into a synthetic joint distribution. We propose sharp MrP bounds instead: the smallest interval containing all estimates of subnational public opinion consistent with the marginal distributions alone. The bounds solve a pair of linear programs and are computationally feasible for typical applications in political science. Applied to two prominent examples in the literature, the bounds are tight enough to be informative and often more accurate than MrP restricted to a coarser, observed joint distribution of census variables. The bounds serve as margin-consistent interval estimates and a diagnostic when researchers use a synthetic joint distribution to construct MrP estimates.

As we show in Appendix A.2, the interval is sharp, i.e., every value inside is attained by some π consistent with the observed margins, and no value outside is attained. It is also the smallest possible interval that does not rely on assumptions beyond those imposed by the observed marginal distributions. The same logic underlies the classical Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds on a joint distribution with fixed marginals (Fréchet, 1951; Hoeffding, 1940; Rüschendorf, 1991).
